blocks.text: An aluminium alloy bicycle frame, a drawn copper wire and a high-strength steel bolt all begin as metals that are soft in their pure, annealed state, because dislocations glide easily. Every method of strengthening a metal does the same thing in a different way: it puts obstacles in the path of dislocations. Which obstacle you choose decides how strong the metal becomes, how much ductility remains and whether the strength survives heating.

blocks.markdown: Plastic flow occurs when dislocations glide, so a metal is strengthened by anything that makes glide harder. The four classic routes are **grain-boundary strengthening** (grain refinement), **solid-solution strengthening**, **precipitation (dispersion) hardening** and **strain (work) hardening**. Each adds a contribution to the yield strength, and each reduces ductility to a different extent.

blocks.caption: Hall-Petch relation: sigma_0 is the friction stress needed to move dislocations in a large single crystal, k_y a material constant (MPa m^1/2) and d the mean grain diameter (m).

blocks.markdown: **Grain boundaries.** A boundary between differently oriented grains stops a dislocation, because its slip plane does not continue into the neighbouring grain. Dislocations pile up against the boundary; the stress concentration at the head of the pile-up is proportional to the pile-up length, which is proportional to the grain size. In a smaller grain the pile-up is shorter, so a higher applied stress is needed to push slip into the next grain. Hence strength rises as $d^{-1/2}$. Grain refinement is unusual because it raises strength and toughness together.

blocks.title: Hall-Petch prediction
blocks.prompt: A low-carbon steel has $\sigma_0=70$ MPa and $k_y=0.60$ MPa m$^{1/2}$. Find the yield strength for mean grain diameters of 25 $\mu$m and 4 $\mu$m.

steps.text: Convert the grain size to metres and compute $d^{-1/2}$ for 25 $\mu$m.
Yield strength for the coarser grain size.

blocks.answer: 190 MPa at 25 micrometres and 370 MPa at 4 micrometres: refining the grain size by a factor of 6 almost doubles the yield strength.

blocks.markdown: **Solid solution and precipitates.** Solute atoms that differ in size from the host atoms distort the lattice, and the strain field around each interacts with the strain field of a dislocation, which makes the dislocation harder to move. The increase grows with the solute content, roughly as the square root of concentration in a simple model, but the effect is moderate (brass is stronger than copper; carbon in iron is exceptionally effective). **Precipitates** are stronger obstacles: a dislocation either shears a small coherent particle or bows between larger particles and leaves a loop around them (the **Orowan** mechanism). The Orowan stress rises as the particle spacing $L$ falls.

blocks.caption: G is the shear modulus, b the Burgers vector magnitude and L the spacing between particles on the slip plane. Closely spaced particles give the greatest strengthening.

rows: Only by grain growth at high temperature
No; stable while the alloy is single phase
Orowan stress Gb/L; peaks at small spacing
Reduced on overageing or dissolving, not by recovery
Yes; removed by recovery and recrystallisation
blocks.caption: Comparison of strengthening routes.

blocks.markdown: **Strain hardening.** Plastic deformation by cold working multiplies dislocations. As the dislocation density $\rho$ rises, dislocations impede one another, and the flow stress increases. The Taylor relation gives the added strength. The amount of cold work is expressed as the percentage reduction in cross-sectional area.

blocks.caption: A0 and Ad are the original and deformed cross-sectional areas; M is about 3.06 for polycrystalline FCC metals, alpha about 0.3, G the shear modulus, b the Burgers vector and rho the dislocation density (m^-2).

blocks.title: Cold working a copper rod
blocks.prompt: A copper rod of diameter 10.0 mm is drawn to 8.0 mm. (i) Find the percentage cold work. (ii) After this drawing the dislocation density is $2\times10^{14}$ m$^{-2}$. With $M=3.06$, $\alpha=0.3$, $G=48$ GPa and $b=0.256$ nm, estimate the increase in yield strength, and the new yield strength if the annealed rod had $\sigma_y=70$ MPa.

steps.text: Area ratio for circular sections is the square of the diameter ratio.
Taylor hardening: first the group $M\alpha Gb$.

blocks.answer: 36 % cold work raises the yield strength by about 160 MPa to about 230 MPa, but the ductility falls sharply.

blocks.markdown: **Effect on ductility and annealing.** Cold work raises the yield and tensile strength, and the hardness, but lowers the elongation (typically a copper rod that elongates 45 % annealed may elongate 10 to 15 % after about 35 % cold work). The stored energy of the extra dislocations can be released by heating, in three stages.

rows: Point defects annihilate; dislocations rearrange into low-energy arrays (polygonisation); residual stress relieved
Small loss of strength; ductility and electrical conductivity partly restored
Recrystallisation (about 0.3 to 0.5 Tm, typically 0.4 Tm in kelvin)
New strain-free grains nucleate and grow, consuming the deformed structure; dislocation density falls by orders of magnitude
Strength and hardness fall to near annealed values; ductility restored
Grain growth (higher temperature or longer time)
Larger grains grow at the expense of smaller ones
Further slight softening; coarse grains reduce Hall-Petch strengthening
blocks.caption: Annealing of a cold-worked metal. Tm is the absolute melting temperature.

blocks.title: Choosing a route
blocks.text: Strain hardening is the cheapest route but is lost on heating. Solid solution and precipitation strengthening survive moderate temperatures, and precipitation can give the highest strength in age-hardenable alloys. Grain refinement is the only route that also improves toughness. In practice the contributions are combined: $\sigma_y\approx\sigma_0+\Delta\sigma_{\text{ss}}+\Delta\sigma_{\text{ppt}}+\Delta\sigma_{\text{wh}}+k_yd^{-1/2}$.

points: Hall-Petch: $\sigma_y=\sigma_0+k_yd^{-1/2}$, so halving the grain size raises the yield strength by a factor of about $\sqrt2$ in the second term; grain refinement raises both strength and toughness.
Solid solution, precipitation (Orowan stress $Gb/L$) and strain hardening (Taylor, $\Delta\sigma\propto\sqrt{\rho}$) all obstruct dislocations; strain hardening is lost on annealing.
%CW $=(A_0-A_d)/A_0\times100$; cold work raises strength and lowers ductility, and recovery, recrystallisation (about $0.4T_m$) and grain growth restore softness and ductility.

questions.stem: A metal has a Hall-Petch friction stress $\sigma_0=40$ MPa and a constant $k_y=0.40$ MPa m$^{1/2}$. Find its yield strength when the mean grain diameter is 16 $\mu$m. Give the answer in MPa.
questions.explanation: The grain size is $16\times10^{-6}$ m, so $d^{-1/2}=250$ m$^{-1/2}$. The Hall-Petch relation gives $\sigma_y=40+0.40\times250=140$ MPa.

questions.stem: An aluminium alloy has $\sigma_0=50$ MPa and $k_y=0.30$ MPa m$^{1/2}$. What mean grain diameter, in micrometres, is needed to give a yield strength of 200 MPa?
questions.explanation: Rearranging, $d^{-1/2}=(\sigma_y-\sigma_0)/k_y=(200-50)/0.30=500$ m$^{-1/2}$. Then $d=1/500^{2}=4.0\times10^{-6}$ m, which is 4.0 micrometres.

questions.stem: Why does the yield strength of a polycrystalline metal increase as the grain size decreases?

options.text: Smaller grains contain more solute atoms, which harden the lattice
Smaller grains have a higher dislocation density before any deformation
Grain boundaries block dislocation glide, and smaller grains give shorter pile-ups, so a higher stress is needed to transmit slip
Smaller grains increase the shear modulus of the metal

questions.correctOptionText: Grain boundaries block dislocation glide, and smaller grains give shorter pile-ups, so a higher stress is needed to transmit slip

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: grain size does not change the solute content.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: annealed polycrystals do not start with a higher dislocation density just from a smaller grain.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the boundaries are obstacles, and the pile-up length scales with the grain size, so the stress needed to propagate slip scales as $d^{-1/2}$.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the shear modulus is a bond property and does not change with grain size.

questions.explanation: Dislocations cannot cross a grain boundary freely, so they pile up against it. The stress concentration at the head of the pile-up grows with its length, which is proportional to the grain size, so a smaller grain needs a higher applied stress; this gives $\sigma_y=\sigma_0+k_yd^{-1/2}$.

questions.stem: In what way does solid-solution strengthening raise the yield strength of an alloy?

options.text: Solute atoms distort the lattice and their strain fields interact with dislocations, making them harder to move
Solute atoms form a second phase of coherent precipitates
Solute atoms increase the grain size, which raises the yield strength
Solute atoms introduce new slip planes of lower resistance

questions.correctOptionText: Solute atoms distort the lattice and their strain fields interact with dislocations, making them harder to move

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the mismatch strain around each solute atom opposes dislocation glide.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: precipitation hardening involves a second phase, not dissolved solute.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: larger grains reduce the Hall-Petch contribution; solute strengthening is independent of the grain size.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: solutes impede, rather than provide, easy slip.

questions.explanation: A substitutional or interstitial solute atom differs in size from the host, creating a local strain field. A moving dislocation must overcome the interaction with this field, so the stress for yielding rises with solute content.

questions.stem: A precipitation-hardened aluminium alloy has particles spaced $L=100$ nm apart on the slip plane. Using the Orowan relation $\Delta\tau=Gb/L$ with $G=26$ GPa and $b=0.286$ nm, what is the added shear stress needed to bow a dislocation between the particles?

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: this corresponds to a spacing ten times larger, 1000 nm.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this corresponds to a spacing ten times smaller, 10 nm.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the result of a unit error of a factor of 285.

questions.explanation: The Orowan stress is $\Delta\tau=Gb/L=26\times10^{9}\times0.286\times10^{-9}/(100\times10^{-9})=7.44\times10^{7}$ Pa, about 74 MPa. Halving the spacing would double it, which is why a fine, dense dispersion is most effective.

questions.stem: A round bar is drawn from a diameter of 12.7 mm to 10.0 mm. What is the percentage cold work?

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: this is the percentage reduction in diameter, not in area.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the ratio of final to initial area, not the reduction.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is the true strain, $\ln(A_0/A_d)\times100$, not the percentage reduction in area.

questions.explanation: Cold work is defined as the reduction in cross-sectional area relative to the original area. For circular sections the area scales as the diameter squared, so the reduction is $1-(10.0/12.7)^{2}=0.380$, or 38.0 %.

questions.stem: As a rule of thumb the recrystallisation temperature of a heavily cold-worked metal is about $0.4T_m$, with $T_m$ the absolute melting temperature. For nickel, with $T_m=1728$ K, estimate the recrystallisation temperature in degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: The estimate is $0.4\times1728=691$ K. Subtracting 273 gives $691-273=418$ C, below which a cold-worked nickel part does not soften appreciably in practical times.

questions.stem: A cold-drawn copper wire is annealed for one hour at a temperature above its recrystallisation temperature. Which statement describes the outcome?

options.text: The wire becomes harder because the heat adds solute atoms
The wire becomes stronger because the dislocation density increases further
The wire is unchanged, since annealing affects only precipitates
The wire softens and regains ductility because new strain-free grains replace the deformed structure

questions.correctOptionText: The wire softens and regains ductility because new strain-free grains replace the deformed structure

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: heating does not add solute and cannot harden a single-phase pure metal.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: annealing lowers the dislocation density; it does not raise it.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: strain hardening is the contribution that annealing removes, so the wire does change.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: recrystallisation removes the dislocation tangles introduced by cold work.

questions.explanation: Cold work stores energy as dislocations. Above the recrystallisation temperature, new strain-free grains nucleate and grow, the dislocation density falls by orders of magnitude, and the wire returns to a soft, ductile state near its annealed properties.

questions.stem: Describe the effect of cold working on the yield strength and ductility of a metal, explain the underlying mechanism, and describe how annealing restores the properties, naming the three stages in order.
markingGuide: Cold work multiplies dislocations and they impede each other, so yield and tensile strength and hardness increase (Taylor: $\Delta\sigma\propto\sqrt{\rho}$)
Ductility (elongation) decreases because the capacity for further strain hardening is used up
Strength increases and ductility decreases with increasing percent cold work
Annealing stage 1: recovery - point defects annihilate, dislocations rearrange, residual stress relieved, small property change
Annealing stage 2: recrystallisation - new strain-free grains form, dislocation density falls, strength falls and ductility is restored (about 0.4 Tm)
Annealing stage 3: grain growth - larger grains grow, further softening
questions.explanation: Cold work stores energy as dislocations, which raises strength at the cost of ductility. Heating lets the metal reduce its stored energy by recovery and recrystallisation, which remove the dislocations and restore softness.

questions.stem: Compare solid-solution strengthening, precipitation hardening and strain hardening as routes to higher strength: state the obstacle for each, the effect on ductility and whether the strength survives heating. A steel has $\sigma_0=40$ MPa and $k_y=0.50$ MPa m$^{1/2}$. Calculate the yield strength at a grain diameter of 10 $\mu$m and the grain size needed to double that strength.
markingGuide: Solid solution: solute atom strain fields; moderate gain and ductility loss; stable on moderate heating
Precipitation hardening: fine particles sheared or bowed around (Orowan, $Gb/L$); can give the largest increases; lost by overageing or dissolving
Strain hardening: dislocation tangles (forest); large ductility loss; removed by recovery and recrystallisation
May note that grain refinement raises strength and toughness together
questions.explanation: The three routes all hinder dislocation glide with different obstacles, so they differ in their ductility penalty and in thermal stability. For the grain-size calculation, $\sigma_y=40+0.5\times316=198$ MPa and doubling requires $d^{-1/2}=712$ m$^{-1/2}$, a grain diameter of about 2 $\mu$m.
